messages.subject: RSFs and density
parts:
Hello,

I have a more philosophical question here, rather than the usual technical questions. In 2013-14, there was discussion in the literature between Royle et al. (Integrating resource selection information with spatial capture–recapture; MEEE 2013) and Efford (Bias from heterogeneous usage of space in spatially explicit capture–recapture analyses; 2014 MEEE) as to how/when RSFs should be incorporated into SCR/SECR models. 

Someone proposed to me the idea that using an RSF-driven estimate of abundance would help resolve this issue / debate (e.g. Boyce and McDonald 1999; you essentially sum the probabilities of use or selection of habitats to estimate N ). I disagree with this suggestion, primarily related to issues of scale, sampling area, and source-sink dynamics in my population of animals.

Does anyone have any insight as to whether this RSF method would be an appropriate approach to the discussion in the literature? I am by no means claiming I will have the answer, just hypothetically speaking, would this be an appropriate approach. 

Hopefully this question is not too vague. Let me know if you need more info,
Annie

messages.subject: Re: RSFs and density
parts:
Your photo was timely indeed!

The question is, can we compare abundance or density estimates from SECR and RSF models to add to the discussion of what role RSFs play in estimating abundance. Here is the scenario:

- As you know, I have bear detection data. I've created density estimates from SECR using habitat covariates. 
- Using the basic Boyce and McDonald framework, I would estimate an RSF from the same habitat covariates and detection data. With the probabilities of selection/use, I would derive N. 

As far as I understand it, these methods are completely different approaches. The RSF is using a use/availability design, whereas the mark/recapture uses the 0/1 from trap locations. So fundamentally, they are comparing different domains (in my opinion). 

Primarily, I am wondering if anyone thinks comparing RSF and SECR estimates of density or abundance is a terrible idea. And why.

Does that clarify the question at all? It is pretty general, I admit

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: RSFs and density
parts:
Hi Annie

Thanks for your amplification. This is a good topic for the group - in fact I have been on the verge of suggesting the group close down because it hasn't been used enough for this sort of thing! And I don't want to hog the space (others may be better placed to answer), but since I've begun...

1. Scale is key: a distinction is drawn between how an animal distributes its activity within its home range (or among resources other than space), which I think is addessed by RSFs, and how animals are distributed across the landscape (in SECR we think of the locations of activity centres). Whether the same rules apply at both scales (which also reflect the time scales on which the 'decisions' are made) is an empirical question with few answers that I know of. RSF may provide a fair hypothesis for landscape-scale drivers of density (distribution of activity centres), but no more than that. See Johnson for 2nd order & 3rd order habitat selection.

2. I don't know what it means to estimate abundance from an RSF. As far as I can see, you can only derive an estimate of N (or density) from the RSF if you know all the bears, and if you know all the bears there's probably no benefit from using RSF to estimate N.

3. Rather than thinking of density merely as a spatial point pattern of activity centres (the SECR approach) we can think of it as the surface that you get from adding all the activity distributions, one on top of another. This has always attracted me for its elegance. The problem is to operationalise it, to estimate the surface from data without bias. The bias comes in because there is uncertainty in the location of each bear, especially the bears never detected from hair DNA, so any surface we generate seems likely to be flatter than the true density surface. (I don't know that this has been formally addressed by anyone).

4. The premise of the Royle et al. MEE paper was that the probability of detection at each detector site depends on how animals distribute their activity within home ranges - hence the RSF connection. I don't think there's much disagreement on that in principle.

Hope this helps you refine the question!
Murray
